column1: # The secret corpus: `scan_secrets` measured as a classifier.
# The secret cases in cases.txt are each written for one pattern family and
# prove that family fires. This file asks the other question — how often the
# gate is wrong on realistic lines in either direction — and gives
# `tests/classifier_corpus.rs` a denominator for precision and recall. The
# numbers in rust/STATUS.md come from here.
# LABELLING RULE (applied by hand, before either the Rust gate or the retired
# Python scanner was run over these lines)
#   secret  the line carries a literal value that would grant access to a
#           system if its characters were real: a vendor-issued key or token,
#           private-key material (a PEM private-key header counts: the key
#           follows it), a password or secret assigned as a literal of eight
#           characters or more, a bearer token, or a URL with an inline password
#           (any length, unless it is a generic word such as `pass` or `test`, or
#           repeats the user name — a documented default like `guest:guest`)
#   clean   anything else: a value read from the environment, a CLI or a
#           secret manager; a placeholder; a hash, checksum, UUID or commit id;
#           a public key or certificate; an identifier or prose that merely
#           names a credential; a value public by design (a publishable key, an
#           OAuth client id); a fixture whose value says it is fake
# A vendor's published documentation example (AWS's `…EXAMPLE` keys, Slack's
# `T00000000/B00000000/XXXX…` webhook) is labelled by its shape, as a secret.
# This repository's own gate tests plant AWS's example key as the canonical
# way to prove the scanner fires without committing a real credential
# devcouncil/stopgate/rigor_end_to_end_test.go), so the gate's contract is to
# Agreement: a blind second labeller agreed on 124/129 lines (Cohen's kappa
# 0.922). Four disagreements were these published examples, resolved by the
# note above; one was the URL length floor, resolved by the URL clause, added
# Every credential-shaped value below is a published example or a padded run
# of fixed characters. None has ever authenticated anything.
# FORMAT: one line per case, four tab-separated columns — label, the path the
# line is added to, a note, and the added line itself (last, so it may contain
# anything but a tab). Lines starting `#` are comments.
